common_name: Reine Victoria Rose (Shell-Pink Repeat-Blooming Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Reine Victoria is a classic Bourbon rose known for its cupped, shell-like carmine-pink blooms and repeat flowering through the season.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, siting it where afternoon air can move freely since the thin petals are prone to balling in damp weather. Bred by Joseph Schwartz in France in 1872 and sometimes called the Shell Rose, it bears cupped, globular, strongly fragrant carmine-pink blooms that fade to soft pink, carried mostly singly on upright, somewhat narrow canes. Unlike the once-blooming Gallicas and Albas, Reine Victoria is a true repeat-blooming Bourbon, flowering in flushes from late spring into fall when fed and watered generously. Watch for blackspot in humid climates and deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush.

common_name: Madame Ernest Calvat Rose (Fragrant Raspberry-Pink Climbing Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring against a pillar, fence, or wall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Ernest Calvat is a pink sport of Madame Isaac Pereire with the same intense fragrance and a more climbing habit.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a pillar, fence, or low wall nearby to support its long, arching canes. Discovered as a sport of Madame Isaac Pereire in France in 1888, it bears very double, quartered blooms of medium pink overlaid with raspberry and violet tones, carrying the same famously intense old-rose fragrance as its parent on up to fifty petals per flower. It is a true repeat-blooming Bourbon, flowering in flushes from late spring into autumn, and performs best where it can be trained horizontally to maximize flowering wood. Feed generously through the growing season and watch for blackspot in humid climates.

common_name: Commandant Beaurepaire Rose (Striped Pink-Violet-and-White Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Commandant Beaurepaire, also sold under its earlier name Panachee d'Angers, is a striped Bourbon rose with flecked pink, violet, and white petals.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room to form a bushy, arching shrub. Bred by Moreau-Robert in France and introduced in 1874, it bears very full, strongly fragrant blooms splashed and striped with light pink, violet-purple, and white flecks, each flower appearing slightly different from the last. It produces its heaviest flush in late spring with lighter, less reliable rebloom later in the season, a trait typical of many striped Bourbon sports. Prune lightly to remove dead or crossing wood after the main flush, since it can be vigorous and somewhat sprawling without occasional shaping.

common_name: Prince Charles Rose (Antique Mauve-and-Crimson Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this antique Bourbon, raised by Julien-Alexandre Hardy before 1837 and distinct from any modern rose of the same name, bears large, richly colored once-blooming flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this early Bourbon tolerates leaner conditions than the later, more refined members of its class. Raised by Julien-Alexandre Hardy in France and dated to around 1837 to 1842, it bears large, double, strongly fragrant blooms that open rose-red to carmine and age toward a smoky mauve, a color progression characteristic of many early Bourbon-China crosses. Unlike most later Bourbons, Prince Charles is essentially once-blooming, producing its single heavy flush in late spring to early summer rather than repeating through the season. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood immediately after flowering to preserve next year's bloom.

common_name: Arthur de Sansal Rose (Dark Crimson-Purple Repeat-Blooming Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Arthur de Sansal is a compact Portland rose valued for its dark crimson-purple, fully double blooms and reliable repeat flowering.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; like other Portlands, it benefits from slightly richer feeding than Gallicas or Albas to sustain repeat bloom on a compact frame. Introduced in France around 1855, it forms an upright, thorny, compact shrub rarely exceeding three and a half feet, bearing richly fragrant, fully double, rosette-shaped flowers in deep crimson-purple that can turn almost violet-gray as they age. It is genuinely repeat-flowering through summer rather than once-blooming, a hallmark trait of the Portland class that distinguishes it from the Gallicas and Damasks it was bred from. Deadhead faded blooms promptly to encourage the next flush, and watch for the dense, short growth habit that makes it well suited to small gardens.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; D'Aguesseau is a vigorous antique Gallica with large, crimson-and-purple, once-blooming flowers.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; D'Aguesseau tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Bred by Jean-Pierre Vibert in France in 1836 and named for the French Chancellor Henri Francois d'Aguesseau, it bears large, full, semi-globular blooms of vivid crimson shaded with purple and a mild, classic old-rose fragrance. Like all Gallicas it is strictly once-blooming, producing a single spectacular flush in late spring before resting for the rest of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood immediately after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ypsilante is an antique Gallica named for the Greek patriot Prince Alexander Ypsilantis, bearing lilac-edged mauve-pink quartered blooms.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ypsilante tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Bred by Jean-Pierre Vibert in France in 1821 and named for the Greek revolutionary general Prince Alexander Ypsilantis, it bears large, full, strongly fragrant flowers in light purple-pink with lilac edges, opening flat and quartered with a neat button eye. As with other Gallicas, bloom comes in a single heavy flush in late spring rather than repeating through the season. Its upright, disease-resistant habit needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Hebe's Lip is a once-blooming antique rose, usually sold as a Damask, with near-white petals delicately edged in cherry-crimson.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; like other antique Damasks, it tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern roses once established. Bred by James Lee in England before 1828, it bears medium to large, single to semi-double, strongly fragrant flowers in near-white delicately edged with cherry-red, a coloring said to recall a kiss on Hebe's lip. It is strictly once-blooming, producing its single flush in late spring to early summer on thorny, dark-foliaged canes, then forming decorative hips later in the season. Trim lightly to remove dead or crossing wood immediately after flowering so as not to sacrifice next year's bloom.

common_name: Gloire de Guilan Rose (Persian Attar-of-Roses Damask)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Gloire de Guilan is a historic Persian Damask long grown in Iran's Guilan province for attar of roses, prized for its intense fragrance.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this sprawling Damask tolerates leaner conditions once established and benefits from a bit of extra room to spread. Rediscovered growing in Iran's Guilan province by Nancy Lindsay in 1949 and of unknown earlier origin, it had long been cultivated there for attar of roses, the essential oil distilled from its intensely fragrant petals. It bears large, loosely double, quartered blooms in light pink, opening in a single heavy flush in late spring with no repeat later in the season, consistent with its Damask heritage. Allow its lax canes to arch naturally and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Madame Plantier Rose (Vigorous Creamy-White Once-Blooming Alba)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Plantier is an exceptionally vigorous, cold-hardy Alba-type rose that can be grown as a large shrub or trained up a support as a short climber.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it ample room or a sturdy support to climb, since it can reach ten feet or more on established, arching canes with few thorns. Bred by Jacques Plantier in France in 1835 from Damask and Musk rose parentage but almost always classed and sold with the Albas for its hardiness and habit, it bears very full, strongly fragrant clusters of cream-white flowers that open from blush buds and age to pure white with a neat button eye. It is strictly once-blooming, producing a spectacular, heavy flush in late spring, then resting for the rest of the season. Exceptionally hardy and tolerant of poor soil, it needs little more than removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Belle Amour Rose (Myrrh-Scented Salmon-Pink Once-Blooming Alba)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Belle Amour is a convent-garden antique rose with an unusual salmon-pink color and a distinctive myrrh fragrance, usually grown with the Albas.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous antique rose tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern roses once established. Found growing on a convent wall at Elboeuf, Normandy, by rose collector Nancy Lindsay before 1940 and introduced in 1950, it bears semi-double, salmon-pink flowers with golden stamens and an unusual myrrh-like fragrance rarely found among the old roses. Its coloring suggests the Albas while its foliage and thorns hint at Damask ancestry, so experts still debate its exact classification. It is once-blooming, flowering in a single abundant flush in late spring, and needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chloris is a very double, pale pink Alba rose that fades gently toward white as its flowers age.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chloris tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Alba. Bred by Jacques-Louis Descemet in France before 1815 and introduced around 1820, it bears small to medium, very double, softly fragrant flowers in light pink that gradually fade to near white as they age, set against the typical gray-green Alba foliage. Like other Albas it is once-blooming, producing a single dependable flush in late spring, and is notably shade-tolerant and disease-resistant for an old rose. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood after flowering, since Albas resent heavy pruning.
